results.title: Hardening Windows Server: Essential tools and techniques for administrators
results.author: IT Experts
results.content:
Securing your infrastructure is a continuous process that requires a layered approach. Hardening Windows Server involves applying security baselines and minimizing the attack surface. It also requires enforcing strict access controls. By leveraging built-in tools and modern authentication methods, you can significantly reduce the risk of compromise. This article summarizes Microsoft’s Windows hardening guide.
Applying security baselines with OSConfig
Security baselines provide a standardized starting point for hardening your servers. Instead of manually configuring hundreds of settings, you can use OSConfig to apply the Microsoft security baseline that matches your server’s role. OSConfig is a security configuration stack that uses a scenario-based approach to deliver and apply desired security measures. It helps prevent configuration drift by detecting and correcting unauthorized changes. You can manage these baselines through PowerShell. Alternatively, you can use Windows Admin Center or Azure Policy.
Leveraging Secured-core hardware
A Secured-core server combines hardware, firmware, and operating system protections to establish a secure foundation before Windows starts. This approach mitigates risks from bootkits and firmware tampering. To use these features, your physical server or virtual machine must support Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0. It also requires UEFI Secure Boot and virtualization-based security. TPM 2.0 provides secure, hardware-backed storage for sensitive keys. UEFI Secure Boot verifies system boot components to prevent malicious rootkits. You can enable the Secured-core scenario using OSConfig or Windows Admin Center.
Minimizing the attack surface
A smaller footprint means fewer vulnerabilities to patch and fewer opportunities for attackers. You should install the Server Core option unless a workload specifically requires the Desktop Experience. Server Core lacks a local graphical interface, which reduces exposed code and maintenance requirements. Additionally, only install the roles and features necessary for the server’s purpose, and remove any unused software.
Managing vulnerabilities and updates
Rapid patching is critical to close known weaknesses before they can be exploited. You must maintain an inventory of your operating system versions. This inventory should also include your applications and firmware versions. Use deployment rings to test updates quickly and ensure you meet remediation deadlines. Tools like Azure Update Manager provide centralized assessment and orchestration for your servers. This helps you monitor update compliance and pending restarts.
Implementing endpoint protection
Microsoft Defender Antivirus and endpoint detection and response provide behavioral monitoring and investigation capabilities. Run Microsoft Defender Antivirus in active mode with real-time protection and cloud-delivered protection enabled. Onboarding your servers to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint gives you centralized visibility. This helps mitigate ransomware and malicious files, as well as suspicious process activity.
Restricting network access and code execution
Windows Defender Firewall should be enabled on all profiles with restrictive rules that only allow required traffic. Furthermore, you can use App Control for Business to define exactly which executables and scripts are allowed to run. You can also control which drivers are permitted. This allowlisting approach is much stronger than relying solely on malware signatures, as it prevents unapproved code from executing.
Securing administrative access
Remote administration paths are attractive targets for attackers. You should disable Remote Desktop Services if it is not needed. When required, protect it with a virtual private network or Remote Desktop Gateway. You must also enforce multifactor authentication and restrict access to authorized groups. To enforce least privilege, provide administrators with standard user accounts for routine work and separate privileged accounts for administrative duties.
Managing local and service credentials
Reusing local administrator passwords across servers allows attackers to move laterally through your network. You can deploy Windows Local Administrator Password Solution to assign unique, automatically rotated passwords to every server. This feature automatically manages and backs up the password of a local administrator account. For services and scheduled tasks, replace static passwords with group Managed Service Accounts or Delegated Managed Service Accounts. These accounts automatically handle password rotation and reduce the risk of credential theft.
Protecting data and auditing activity
Encrypting your operating system and data volumes with BitLocker ensures that physical theft or offline access does not compromise your data. BitLocker is a volume encryption feature that protects data at rest. Additionally, you must configure detailed auditing to record security-relevant activity, such as authentication failures and privilege use. Forward these logs to a centralized platform like Azure Monitor or a Security Information and Event Management system to detect and alert on suspicious behavior across your environment. A Security Information and Event Management system provides real-time analysis of security alerts generated by applications and network hardware.
Conclusion
Hardening Windows Server is a multifaceted effort that requires minimizing the attack surface and enforcing strict access controls. It also requires maintaining continuous visibility. By applying role-specific baselines and leveraging hardware security features, you can build a resilient infrastructure. Managing credentials effectively is also a key component of this process. Regularly testing your configurations and recovery procedures ensures that your defenses remain effective against evolving threats.
results.summary:
Microsoft’s comprehensive Windows Server hardening guide outlines essential strategies for securing infrastructure, including applying security baselines, leveraging hardware-based protections, and enforcing strict access controls to mitigate modern cyber threats.

### Key Points
- Use OSConfig to apply standardized security baselines and prevent configuration drift across server environments.
- Enable Secured-core hardware features, including TPM 2.0 and UEFI Secure Boot, to protect against firmware-level tampering.
- Minimize the attack surface by deploying Server Core and removing unnecessary roles, features, and software.
- Implement Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) to automate unique password rotation for local accounts.
- Utilize App Control for Business to restrict execution to authorized scripts, drivers, and applications only.
- Centralize security monitoring by forwarding audit logs to Azure Monitor or a Security Information and Event Management system.

### Why it Matters
Implementing these hardening measures significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access and lateral movement within a network. By adopting a layered security approach, organizations can better protect sensitive data and maintain operational resilience against evolving cyberattacks.

results.author: bringatrailer
results.content:
This Week’s Weird and Wonderful—July 24, 2026
We’re just off of two weeks with two huge events, and there are even more coming up. We can imagine that you, like us, might need to spend some time out of the sun, and to help you reduce your exposure to harmful UV rays, we have concocted this list of the most interesting and unique cars on BaT to keep you inside and in front of your computer, where it’s safe. Today we have a slew of prewar beauties, a golf cart from another galaxy, a ’50s fiberglass father-and-son duo, and our first ever sailboat, to mention just a few of the vehicular curiosities below.
Enjoy this week’s Weird and Wonderful, and head over to our live auctions page when you’re done to finish maxing out your screen time.
A repulsorlift engine with three supplementary air-cooled thrust turbines sounds exotic, but a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, the Sorosuub X-34 Landspeeder was the equivalent of a well-used Subaru—trusty and capable, if decidedly unsexy. The kind of vehicle that would find an appreciative audience in the Galactic Outer Rim equivalent of Bring a Trailer. This replica was built not for the harsh sands of Tatooine, but for the manicured greens of the Florida golf course. It cuts a conspicuous silhouette on the front nine, but that’s fine so long as you’re not trying to smuggle droids off the planet.
This Hispano-Suiza J12 hadn’t been completed by the time most of its surviving brethren were on their first or second refurbishment. While most J12 production took place at the firm’s Paris branch, this example was reportedly started at the Barcelona facility, but then left incomplete for 40 years! While its backstory remains shrouded in mystery, chassis 23452 eventually received a Carrosserie Pourtout body originally meant for a 1924 H6B, and today it remains a non-running (but gorgeous-looking) project being sold by Local Partner @1600veloce.
Gabriel Voisin was known for bold Art Deco “rational” designs, which translated his purposeful and elegant aircraft design techniques into the world of terrestrial transport. The C7, while beautiful, achieved function through thoughtful application of technology. Its low-slung aluminum monocoque body was lightweight and corrosion-resistant, with a spacious greenhouse for outward visibility. It managed to accommodate three large storage trunks atop its short 113″ wheelbase, and featured manually-retracting sliding side windows (another lightweight solution), vacuum-assisted mechanical brakes, a wide-set rear spotlight (to illuminate the road without blinding oncoming traffic), and cabin that was luxurious, ergonomic, and simple all at the same time. Its airplane-style dash would look right at home with a Vickers machine gun mounted on top.
Paul Newman gets top billing here, but just as interesting is that this IMSA GTP car was built by Gordon Spice and Ray Bellm, who had won the WSC team and constructors championships for the previous two years in the lower C2 class. Their SE89P, a C1 challenger, logged two top-ten finishes in its first year of competition. By the late 2000s, it was a regular on the vintage racing circuit, and is fresh off a trip up the hill at Goodwood. What we particularly like about this car (even more than the alternate Applebees livery!) is its combination of high-tech materials with a big aluminum pushrod Chevy V8—a Group C prototype with the heart of a Can Am racer.
Here’s one potential solution to the seemingly never-ending housing crisis, and it was actually built nearly a hundred years ago—a 1927 Studebaker House Car! A California-based company plopped their aluminum dwelling over a Studebaker Special Six chassis in period, but this example was renovated more recently with features one might expect in stylish tiny house—exposed wooden ceiling and cabinetry, dual 10-gallon water tanks with a hot water unit, a refrigerator, and air conditioning. So it turns out you can drive your house, and better yet—this one gets its power from a big Ford 460ci V8.
Back in March 1992, former Car and Driver Editor-in-Chief William Jeanes mentioned that Ferrari put more time and development into the 512 TR than most small automakers ever put into their company, period. The goal at the time was to transform the Testarossa from a GT to a true supercar (though that didn’t stop editor John Phillips from road tripping one from coast to coast a few months later). This particular 512 TR, however, went straight past “supercar” and headed for the track, outfitted with an aluminum Koenig Specials body kit and a roll cage, and was campaigned by the late racer William Hubbell. We have to say that it looks somewhat understated on track; it’s probably the first time the word has ever been uttered about a TR.
1931 Franklin Series 15 Model 153 Deluxe Oxford Sedan and 1930 Hudson Great Eight Brougham
Anyone trying to make a gangster movie would do well to shop on Bring a Trailer this week. The number of prewar stunners our sellers have brought to the site is astounding, and we love to see it. The CCCA-awarded Franklin above is an air-cooled luxury sedan built in Syracuse, New York, with a capacious rear cabin outfitted more like an upscale lounge than an automobile. With 100 horsepower on tap, the Jazz Age Franklin was a hot number that could really shake a leg. Unfortunately, the company went all-in on a super-size redesign in 1932 and ended up bankrupting itself.
Hudson came sailing into the Great Depression with plenty of wind at their backs. Coming off of a 300,000-car year in 1929, they introduced a revamped lineup for 1930 with power from a new, smooth-running straight-eight like the one in this colorful Great Eight Brougham. The cars were well-received, but production dropped to 113,000 cars during these famously tough times. The Great Eight ended up being a one-year offering, as Hudson executives tried to stem the loss of sales with “clever” marketing: the model was renamed the “Greater Eight” for 1931 and 1932.
Another in the bumper crop of prewar machinery this week is this elegant Chrysler CG Imperial Convertible Victoria, hailed as Chrysler’s crown jewel in its day. Those distinguished enough to own such a fine piece of machinery typically went with factory coachwork by LeBaron, while just six cars wore Convertible Victoria coachwork by Waterhouse. This example of the latter held court in the lobby of the Chrysler building in New York before changing hands several times throughout the decades on its way to the current owner in 2008. It was refurbished in the early 2000s, and comes with more trophies than will fit into the trunk.
With Bill Stroppe Baja Broncos, it’s all in the details. This particular rig has quite the ownership history—it was first purchased by an employee of Bill Stroppe, Harold Allen, before it found its way in 1977 to Off-Road Motorsports Hall of Fame inductee Rod Hall, who had previously won the Baja 1000 overall in 1969 aboard another Stoppe Bronco with Jim Fricker. The seller mentions that Hall used the truck as a family rig, pulling a Starcraft Swinger camper trailer and crossing the border into Mexico a few times—it doesn’t get any better than that.
The “3=6” model designation originated as a piece of marketing. The idea was that DKW’s three-cylinder engine, with its two-stroke combustion cycle, would have made power roughly equivalent to the typical six-cylinder of the era, and the claim ended up becoming the car’s model name. Whatever the numerical inaccuracies, this was a handsome, humble, well-made, well-mannered economy car with an exhaust note like Zeus’s own chainsaw. DKW was the drummer in the four-brand outfit called Auto Union, and the car was later marketed under the Auto Union marque as the Saxomat 1000 with a larger 981cc engine.
Honorable Mentions
1950s Woodill Brushfire and Woodill Wildfire Project
Blanchard Robert “Woody” Woodill teamed up with Bill Tritt to design the Woodill Wildfire in the 1950s. They also created a 5/8-scale children’s car, the Brushfire, to capture an even bigger market of smaller people. Unfortunately neither model caught fire, with a limited number of each made.
But today, we have both models together on BaT! The Brushfire minicar is offered by @zagato62 out of California, while @Frog49 is back with the Wildfire project he purchased back in 2024.
Our favorite JDM vehicle model names all have something in common: they could function as suitable titles of 1990s Adam Sandler movies. The Deliboy—see? It works!
BaT is (ahem) sailing into uncharted territory with the first wind-powered vehicle we’ve ever listed. The yawl configuration—two masts with the rearmost (mizzenmast) far aft—allows the boat to be operated by a one- or two-person crew. Hats off to our colleagues on the production staff, who did a great job with the nautical terminology.
Thanks for checking out this edition of the Weekly Weird & Wonderful! Follow this page to get updates when new installments post, and tell what caught your eye or what you think we’ve left out!
results.summary:
Bring a Trailer’s latest "Weird and Wonderful" collection features a diverse array of unique vehicles, ranging from a Star Wars landspeeder replica to rare prewar luxury automobiles.

### Key Points
- The auction list includes a custom-built Sorosuub X-34 Landspeeder replica designed for golf course use.
- A rare 1930s Hispano-Suiza J12 project car, originally started in Barcelona, is being offered by partner @1600veloce.
- The selection features a 1927 Studebaker House Car, a vintage mobile home renovated with modern tiny-house amenities.
- Racing history is represented by a 1989 Spice SE89P IMSA GTP car and a track-modified Ferrari 512 TR with a Koenig Specials body kit.
- The collection includes a rare Chrysler CG Imperial Convertible Victoria with coachwork by Waterhouse, formerly displayed in the Chrysler Building.
- Bring a Trailer has expanded its inventory to include its first-ever sailboat, a yawl-configured vessel designed for small-crew operation.

### Why it Matters

Another bearish factor was President Trump’s new tariff regime on 60 nations and his threat of new EU tariffs in retaliation for the EU’s $1 billion fine for Alphabet. Also, the markets are worried that the US might expand its military attacks on Iran, as President Trump said he is considering.

President Trump late Thursday announced broad tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% on 60 nations, replacing the 10% global import tax that expired. The new tariffs are based on trade authority under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 tied to a claim of forced labor in supply chains. Mr. Trump had to seek new trade authority after the Supreme Court struck down his so-called reciprocal tariffs in February. Mr. Trump replaced the reciprocal tariffs with a 10% global import tax that expired Friday.
The new forced-labor tariffs exclude some key items such as fuel, foods, fertilizer, and products covered by the North American trade agreement with Mexico and Canada. The new tariffs also exclude automobiles, metals, and drugs, which are covered by tariffs based on a different trade authority. The Trump administration has a raft of other Section 301 investigations underway that could be used to impose more tariffs in the future, stacked on top of today’s forced-labor tariff.

Oil prices fell as oil tankers continued to move through the Red Sea despite Houthi threats, with some oil tankers turning off their location transponders.

The Houthis have vowed to blockade shipping linked to Saudi Arabia and warned shipowners against calling at the nation's ports. results.content:
On Wednesday's episode of Mad Money, Jim Cramer labeled a recent security incident a "watershed moment" for the technology industry, making a case for CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD). Cramer emphasized that the rise of rogue AI agents creates an urgent threat vector requiring specialized enterprise protection:
This morning, we had a watershed moment we've all been waiting for. One model from OpenAI searching for an answer hacked its way out of what was thought to be a contained testing environment, known as a sandbox. Then went online and hacked into Hugging Face's server. Come on, this was amazing. Then Hugging Face used the Chinese model to stop it. I mean, this is insane. It means that the impossible has indeed happened. Agents went rogue... I think this is one of the biggest stories out there. In a world where AI agents can go rogue, what do you do? Well, you should just buy the stock of CrowdStrike. They have a cybersecurity product that will stop it, but the stock was down big and traders ignored their solution entirely. So much for that idea.
Autonomous Cyber Threats and the Falcon Platform Moat
The event highlighted by Cramer marks a shift in the cybersecurity landscape. When AI models break out of virtual sandboxes and breach external infrastructure, traditional static firewalls and legacy security software prove ineffective. CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:CRWD) proprietary Falcon platform, powered by cloud-native threat intelligence and real-time behavioral analytics, is specifically engineered to detect and contain autonomous anomalous behaviors across endpoints, cloud workloads, and identity systems before damage can spread.
Recently, the stock declined due to AI worries, especially after news of Anthropic's Mythos platform came to light. However, Cramer has addressed these worries time and time again. During the April 21 episode, Cramer called AI a "tailwind" for cybersecurity companies like CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD) instead of a "headwind." Furthermore, he highlighted the stock's comeback from those worries during the July 6 episode, as he stated:
A few months back, in the dead of winter, Anthropic let people know it was developing the best cybersecurity software, the best. I don't know why everything that Anthropic says gets somehow turned into gospel. But the ensuing stories crushed two cybersecurity stocks I happen to like very much: Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike. Oh, it was brutal. So what did we do? We brought George Kurtz on the show, the CEO of CrowdStrike, several times to say that, point blank, Anthropic simply wouldn't be able to offer a truly competing product; that it would be up to the cybersecurity companies to do it, that it would be up to CrowdStrike.
No one listened except perhaps the CNBC Investing Club… And the club caught nearly a double in CrowdStrike when people realized that not only would Anthropic not be able to offer a workable product, no insurer would insure any company that used an AI model and also provided cybersecurity for that model. Coverage will be denied. Anthropic will cause more cyber hacks than it will prevent unless it's matched with a CrowdStrike or a Palo Alto Networks.

results.title: Guillermo del Toro Promises ‘Absolutely No Goddamn AI’ on ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ 3D Re-Release
results.author: Charisma Madarang
results.content:
As Hollywood continues to soften its stance on artificial intelligence, Guillermo del Toro remains immovable in his opposition to AI in cinema.
	The Oscar-winning filmmaker returned to San Diego Comic-Con to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Pan’s Labyrinth. When discussing its upcoming 3D re-release in theaters, premiering Oct. 9, del Toro assured fans that “absolutely no goddamn AI” was used to convert the movie.
“It’s much more expensive. I don’t care. The thing is, what we’re protecting is the beauty and the redeeming power of art. It’s not about who gets the job,” said del Toro to cheers from the crowd. “We are protecting a lineage of art. If we cut a generation of people from learning their craft, you’re cutting the rest of the history of that medium away from them for what?”
When speaking to NPR last year, del Toro made it clear that he wasn’t interested in the tech and said he’d “rather die” than use AI. “AI, particularly generative AI — I am not interested, nor will I ever be interested,” he told NPR. “I’m 61, and I hope to be able to remain uninterested in using it at all until I croak. … The other day, somebody wrote me an email, said, ‘What is your stance on AI?’ And my answer was very short. I said, ‘I’d rather die.'”
	Pan’s Labyrinth, a Spanish-language film released in 2006 and praised for its gothic surrealism, garnered $83 million worldwide at the box office and three Academy Awards for Best Cinematography, Best Art Direction, and Best Makeup.

results.title: A federal appeals court rejects Trump's bid to keep in place the $100,000 H-1B visa fee
results.author: Katherine Li,Kelsey Vlamis
results.content:
President Donald Trump's plans for H-1B visas are running into legal roadblocks.
A federal appeals court on Friday refused to revive Trump's $100,000 fee on new H-1B work visas, dealing another setback to the administration's effort to dramatically raise the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers.
The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to pause a lower court ruling that blocked the fee while the administration appeals. A three-judge panel said the government failed to show it was likely to succeed in arguing that the president had the authority to impose the charge.
The decision leaves in place a June ruling by US District Judge Leo Sorokin, who said the fee amounted to a tax, which falls under Congress's authority to authorize, rather than the president's.
"Here, the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," Sorokin wrote.
Trump announced the fee in September 2025 as part of a broader immigration crackdown, stating at the time the H-1B program "has been deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement, American workers with lower-paid, lower-skilled labor."
Brian Hunt, an immigration policy compliance lawyer with Fragomen, Del Rey, Bernsen & Loewy, LLP, told Business Insider that it's unclear how many people this court decision will affect, because most US employers hire H-1B workers who are already in the US.
"In light of the 100k fee, there are some workers who were about to lose their job offer but can now get a visa after all," Hunt said.
The H-1B program issues around 65,000 visas each year, plus another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees, and is widely used by technology companies to recruit overseas talent. Before Trump's policy, employers generally paid between about $2,000 and $5,000 in visa-related fees.
Court filings show the steep increase has sharply reduced demand. By mid-February, US Citizenship and Immigration Services had received few payments of the new fee.
The lawsuit challenging the fee was brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
results.summary:
A federal appeals court has blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to impose a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, ruling the charge likely exceeds presidential executive authority.

### Key Points
- The 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request to pause a lower court injunction against the $100,000 visa fee.
- US District Judge Leo Sorokin previously ruled the fee functions as a tax, which requires congressional authorization rather than executive action.
- The H-1B program typically issues 85,000 visas annually to high-skilled workers, primarily supporting the technology sector.
- Twenty Democratic state attorneys general filed the lawsuit challenging the fee, which had significantly reduced visa demand since its September 2025 announcement.
- Standard H-1B visa-related costs typically range between $2,000 and $5,000, making the proposed $100,000 charge a substantial increase for employers.

### Why it Matters
This ruling limits the administration's ability to unilaterally reshape immigration policy through high-cost financial barriers. It provides immediate relief to technology companies and foreign workers who rely on the H-1B program to maintain essential staffing levels.

results.title: The Truth About Fake USB Drives Circulating Online
results.author: News On Japan
results.content:
TOKYO - Low-cost USB drives advertised online with enormous storage capacities are exposing users to the risk of lost data, malware infections and information theft, with tests finding that some products contain only a fraction of the memory shown on their labels.
USB-related security breaches have become a growing concern for companies and public organizations. Factories, research laboratories, hospitals and other facilities requiring strict security often operate computer systems disconnected from the internet. When outside data or software must be transferred to those systems, USB drives are commonly used, creating an opening for malware to enter otherwise isolated networks.
The greatest risks may lie in products that appear most attractive to ordinary buyers: USB drives offering large capacities at unusually low prices through major online shopping platforms.
A Nikkei investigation previously revealed that the Ground Self-Defense Force had used a counterfeit Chinese USB drive infected with malware. The product had been distributed through an online retailer widely used by the public, raising concerns that similar devices may have been purchased by individuals, companies and other organizations.
Internal Ground Self-Defense Force documents obtained by Nikkei showed that the infected USB drive had been used for nearly a year before the problem was detected. The documents included a detailed analysis of the device and the malware infection.
Because the USB drive had been acquired through Amazon, the risk was not limited to the Self-Defense Forces. Nikkei reporters purchased a selection of inexpensive USB drives online, including products sold under the same brand used by the Ground Self-Defense Force, and examined their true capacity.
Half of the 10 types tested had falsified storage capacities.
One device was advertised as holding about 1 terabyte, but its actual capacity was less than 0.01% of that amount. Other drives displayed less storage than advertised and began deleting previously saved data when users attempted to write more information than the devices could physically hold.
To examine how common such products are, a separate 4-terabyte USB drive was purchased online for 5,380 yen, a price far below that of a legitimate device with comparable capacity.
The drive was taken to AI Data, a company specializing in data recovery, for testing. Before examining the newly purchased product, technicians demonstrated the process using another USB drive already confirmed to be fraudulent.
When connected to a computer, the device appeared to have a capacity of 500 gigabytes. A diagnostic test completed about 10 seconds later identified suspected capacity falsification and found that the drive contained only 58.2 gigabytes, or roughly 10% of the advertised amount.
The missing storage did not exist physically. Software in the USB drive's controller had been manipulated to make the computer display memory that was not actually present.
The device could appear to accept files normally, misleading users into believing their photographs, documents and other data had been safely stored. When they later tried to open the files, however, the information could not be read because it had never been properly saved.
Testing of the 4-terabyte USB drive purchased for the investigation produced a writing error, meaning the device became unable to accept the test data. The product failed during the examination.
Technicians then dismantled the casing to inspect its internal components. Hidden inside was a microSD card with a capacity of only 64 gigabytes, a tiny fraction of the 4 terabytes displayed when the drive was connected to a computer.
The investigation also found that some suspicious products were sold in small metal cases, a form of packaging that technicians said frequently appeared with capacity-falsified devices, although legitimate products may also use similar containers.
The danger extends beyond fraudulent memory capacity. Inexpensive USB drives may also contain malware planted by hacker groups, according to the Nikkei journalist who uncovered the Ground Self-Defense Force case.
Large numbers of companies, organizations and individuals purchase inexpensive USB drives, creating opportunities for malicious devices to eventually reach businesses or institutions holding confidential information. Once connected to a computer, an infected drive could install malware and steal sensitive data.
The strategy may rely on distributing many compromised devices and waiting for one to be purchased by a valuable target.
Consumers and organizations were advised to avoid buying unusually cheap USB drives through online marketplaces and instead purchase products from established manufacturers through electronics retailers or other trusted physical stores.
Such products may cost more, but retailers generally source devices from manufacturers they consider reliable, reducing the risk of malware infections, falsified capacity and the loss of irreplaceable files.
Many consumers interviewed said they no longer used USB drives because they stored most data in cloud services. However, the report noted that cloud storage also carries serious security risks, although the source material ended before those risks were explained.
Source: テレ東BIZ
results.summary:
Low-cost USB drives sold on major online marketplaces are frequently found to have falsified storage capacities and may contain malware, posing significant security risks to individuals and organizations.

### Key Points
- Investigations revealed that half of the tested inexpensive USB drives displayed falsified storage capacities, with some holding less than 0.01% of the advertised memory.
- Fraudulent devices often use manipulated controller software to report fake capacities, leading to permanent data loss when users attempt to save files.
- A Nikkei investigation confirmed that the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force inadvertently used a malware-infected USB drive purchased through a major online retailer.
- Technical inspections of a 4-terabyte drive revealed it contained only a 64-gigabyte microSD card, highlighting the physical discrepancy between marketing and reality.
- Security experts warn that these devices can act as vectors for malware, potentially compromising isolated computer networks in hospitals, laboratories, and government facilities.

### Why it Matters
These fraudulent products create a significant security vulnerability by allowing malware to bypass air-gapped systems and steal sensitive data from high-value targets. Consumers and organizations are advised to avoid unusually cheap hardware and source storage devices exclusively from established manufacturers through trusted retailers.

results.title: SpaceX’s Starship test successfully reaches space, deploys satellites after record-breaking IPO
results.author: Editorial Team
results.content:
SpaceX’s Starship test successfully reaches space, deploys satellites after record-breaking IPO
Flight 13 marks the company's first Starship mission since going public, deploying 20 next-gen Starlink satellites in a suborbital test
SpaceX just pulled off its 13th Starship flight test, sending the world’s largest rocket to space and deploying 20 Starlink V3 satellites along the way. The July 24 launch from Starbase, Texas, was the company’s first Starship mission since its blockbuster IPO in June, and it went about as well as shareholders could have hoped.
For a company that raised approximately $86 billion in what became the largest IPO in history, sticking the landing on a high-profile test flight is the kind of thing that keeps investor confidence from evaporating.
What actually happened during Flight 13
The V3 Starship/Super Heavy vehicle launched on a suborbital trajectory, carrying 20 operational Starlink V3 satellites. These were the first fully functional V3 variants ever carried by Starship, designed to test enhanced network capabilities and faster speeds for SpaceX’s satellite internet constellation.
The mission hit several technical milestones. SpaceX successfully relit its Raptor engines while in space, a capability that’s essential for future orbital missions and any serious talk about Mars. The upper stage achieved what the company described as its “softest splashdown” to date, executing a controlled descent into the Indian Ocean.
The Super Heavy booster completed a water landing in the Gulf of America. Initial launch attempts were aborted due to engine issues before the successful flight.
The road to Flight 13
Across 12 prior Starship flights, SpaceX logged 8 successes and 5 failures, according to Wikipedia’s tracking. Flight 12, conducted on May 22, 2026, was the first time SpaceX deployed any Starlink satellites from Starship, though those were modified units primarily intended for heat shield inspection rather than full network service. Flight 13 represented a significant step forward by carrying production-grade V3 hardware.
Why crypto and tech investors should care
The Starlink angle is particularly relevant for anyone tracking the intersection of technology infrastructure and decentralized networks. Starlink V3 satellites promise significantly enhanced speed and capacity, expanding the reach of high-bandwidth internet to areas where traditional infrastructure doesn’t exist. Decentralized networks, blockchain validators, and crypto mining operations in remote locations all benefit from more reliable, faster satellite internet coverage.
SpaceX still hasn’t achieved rapid turnaround between Starship flights, which is the ultimate unlock for cost reduction. The company needs to go from months between tests to days or weeks between operational flights for the economics to truly transform the launch industry.
For investors watching SpaceX’s public market performance, the next milestones to track include whether the company attempts a booster tower catch on upcoming flights, how quickly it can iterate toward Flight 14, and whether the deployed Starlink V3 satellites perform as expected in operational testing.
results.summary:
SpaceX successfully completed its 13th Starship test flight from Starbase, Texas, deploying 20 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites while demonstrating critical engine relight capabilities during a controlled suborbital mission.

### Key Points
- SpaceX launched the Starship/Super Heavy vehicle on July 24, marking the company's first mission since its record-breaking $86 billion IPO.
- The mission successfully deployed 20 operational Starlink V3 satellites, designed to provide enhanced network speeds and capacity.
- Engineers successfully relit the Raptor engines in space, a technical milestone required for future orbital and Mars-bound missions.
- The upper stage achieved a controlled descent into the Indian Ocean, while the Super Heavy booster completed a water landing in the Gulf of America.

### Why it Matters
- The successful deployment of V3 hardware signals a major advancement in global satellite internet infrastructure, offering high-bandwidth connectivity to remote regions. This progress directly impacts the scalability of decentralized networks and remote digital operations that rely on consistent, high-speed satellite data links.

results.title: Ethereum Builder Says CLARITY ACT Rumors May Be Potential Catalyst For Next Crypto Market Dump
results.author: Olivia Brooke
results.content:
The next cryptocurrency market dump could be spearheaded by a myriad of factors across the crypto market as well as the broader global finance market. While it remains unknown what the exact catalyst could be, Crypto market players are already outlining their predictions in an attempt to inform fellow market participants.
In a recent post shared to X, formerly Twitter, a prominent Ethereum builder pointed to the widely discussed and highly anticipated CLARITY ACT as a potential driver of the crypto market’s next dip.
Econar, a long-time Ethereum builder and crypto personality, took to X to share that a weak price rally—a fake out—may be witnessed as rumors of CLARITY ACT potentially being passed intensify.
If, however, the ACT is not passed, a continuous downward trend could send the market to lower lows.
“Crypto is going to do that thing where we barely pump on rumor of something good happening (CLARITY), and then when it doesn’t happen, despite the pass not even being properly priced in, we will dump lower than we would have dumped if nothing ever happened.” He wrote.
Econar’s position speaks to the market trend of “buying the rumour and selling the news,” a pattern in the crypto community often led by increased market hype on a specific product, event or potential development, with no concrete evidence in sight.
In such cases, market players have historically responded to delays and weaker-than-expected performances with profit-taking and disappointment, often resulting in a sell-off.
The industry players’ concerns come as conversations centering the CLARITY ACT skyrocket within Crypto spaces, as a series of events suggests that the bill could be well on its way to becoming law.
Not long after the Senate Banking Committee advanced the bill on May 14th, House Financial Services held a field hearing in New York City on how CLARITY unlocks innovation on July 17th.
The bill remains on the Senate Legislative Calendar at this time, with a 43% to 60% odds of passage before the August recess, according to Galaxy Digital.
results.summary:
Ethereum developer Econar warns that the proposed CLARITY Act could trigger a cryptocurrency market downturn if the legislation fails to meet investor expectations following recent speculative price rallies.

### Key Points
- Ethereum builder Econar suggests that market participants may be overestimating the impact of the CLARITY Act, leading to a potential "buy the rumor, sell the news" sell-off.
- The Senate Banking Committee officially advanced the CLARITY Act on May 14, followed by a House Financial Services field hearing in New York City on July 17.
- Galaxy Digital estimates the probability of the bill passing before the upcoming August recess currently ranges between 43% and 60%.
- Market analysts fear that if the legislation fails to pass, the resulting disappointment could drive cryptocurrency prices to new lows.

### Why it Matters
This situation highlights how legislative uncertainty and speculative trading patterns continue to drive volatility within the broader digital asset market. Investors are closely monitoring the bill's progress as its potential enactment could significantly influence regulatory frameworks and institutional sentiment toward cryptocurrency innovation.

results.title: Paramount agrees to pause Warner Bros deal while court case plays out
results.author: Al Jazeera Staff
results.content:
Paramount Skydance has agreed to pause its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery until after a federal judge rules on states’ challenge to the deal, according to court papers.
The delay, filed in court on Friday, could cost Paramount Skydance about $7m a day in fees it agreed to pay Warner Bros shareholders if the merger does not close by September 30.

- list 4 of 4US small businesses challenge Trump’s new forced labour tariffs
“We look forward to proving our case at trial,” Paramount’s spokesperson said.
Twelve states, led by California, sued on July 13, arguing the deal would “extinguish competition” in Hollywood and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly moviegoers and cable customers. Paramount has called the states’ claims meritless and pledged to “vigorously defend” its merger.
“Halting this merger while our case proceeds is a critical victory in our efforts to uphold the law and protect the film and television industries,” said New York Attorney General Letitia James, who is suing to block the deal.
Friday’s move arrives just days after US District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted a temporary restraining order requested by the states to freeze the transaction for several weeks.
The companies agreed to pause the deal until five days after the judge rules on the merits of the case, or June 1, 2027, whichever comes first. Paramount could owe as much as $1.7bn in ticking fees to Warner Bros shareholders if the deal is delayed until then.
Similar merger challenges have taken an average of eight months for a judge to rule, a review of recent cases by the Reuters news agency has found.
There have also been concerns over a media stranglehold as the merger would have brought CNN, currently owned by Warner Bros, under the umbrella of Paramount. The latter already owns CBS, which has seen a fair amount of turmoil amid allegations of bias in favour of US President Donald Trump under the leadership of CEO David Ellison, whose father, tech billionaire Larry Ellison, is a Trump ally.
results.summary:
Paramount Skydance has agreed to pause its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery until a federal judge rules on a multistate lawsuit challenging the media merger's legality.

### Key Points
- Twelve states, led by California and New York, sued to block the merger, claiming it would reduce competition and consumer choice in the entertainment industry.
- US District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a temporary restraining order, prompting the companies to halt the transaction until June 1, 2027, or until a court ruling.
- Paramount Skydance faces potential "ticking fees" of approximately $7 million per day, which could total $1.7 billion if the deal remains delayed.
- The merger would consolidate major media assets, including CBS and CNN, raising concerns regarding market concentration and editorial independence.

### Why it Matters
This legal standoff highlights increasing regulatory scrutiny over media consolidation and the potential for antitrust litigation to derail multibillion-dollar corporate mergers. The outcome will set a significant precedent for how federal courts evaluate competition in the evolving film and television landscape.

results.title: DuRoBo Krono: The Pocket-Sized Android E-Ink Hub That Dials Down Distraction and Powers Up Focus
results.author: Scott Webster
results.content:
The DuRoBo Krono is a 6.13-inch Android ePaper focus hub from DuRoBo, a brand built around the idea that your reading and thinking device should help you slow down, not speed up. Priced at $279.99, the Krono positions itself as a compact, distraction-free companion for readers, note-takers, and anyone who wants a pocket-sized device that does more than just store books. If you’ve been looking for a way to reclaim some focus without giving up the flexibility of a proper Android device, this one deserves a close look.
What It Is
The Krono is a compact Android e-reader and idea-capture device. It’s not a phone or a tablet, but something in between. It runs Android 15 on an octa-core processor with 6 GB of RAM and 128 GB of onboard storage, which gives it the horsepower to handle the Google Play Store, productivity apps, reading platforms, and more.
The display is a 6.13-inch E Ink Carta 1200 panel at 300 PPI with a resolution of 824 × 1648, delivering crisp, paper-like text that’s easy on the eyes. At 154 × 80 × 9 mm and approximately 173 g, it fits in a pocket and doesn’t ask much of your bag. What sets the Krono apart from the growing crowd of Android e-readers is its mechanical Smart Dial, a physical rotary control that gives the device a tactile identity all its own.
Key Features
Smart Dial — The Krono’s most distinctive element is a mechanical rotary dial on the left side of the device. It supports four interaction types: single press, double press, press and hold, and rotation. Each maps to a different action depending on context — turning pages while reading, scrolling while browsing, adjusting frontlight brightness on the home screen, or launching voice capture with a long press. It’s a thoughtful physical interface that reduces how often you need to reach for the touchscreen.
E Ink Carta 1200 Display with Adjustable Frontlight — The 300 PPI Carta 1200 panel is among the sharpest available in this size class, and the dual-tone adjustable frontlight means you can dial in comfortable reading conditions whether you’re in bright daylight or a dark room.
Spark Voice and Text Capture — Spark is DuRoBo’s built-in idea-capture tool, accessible via a press-and-hold on the Smart Dial from virtually anywhere on the device. Voice mode records spoken thoughts and converts them to text via speech-to-text transcription, with an option to generate AI summaries of longer recordings. Text mode handles situations where speaking isn’t practical.
Libby AI Assistant — A double press of the Smart Dial opens Libby AI, the device’s built-in assistant for quick questions and information lookups — without pulling out your phone.
Open Android 15 Platform — Full Google Play Store access means you’re not locked into a single reading ecosystem. Install Kindle, Kobo, Libby, Pocket, or any other app that works on Android. The Krono handles it.
Axis Lighting System — Six subtle “breathing lights” on the back of the device can activate during scheduled reading reminders or focus sessions, offering a quiet visual cue to return to what you were doing. It’s a small detail, but one that reflects DuRoBo’s broader design philosophy.
Who It’s For
The Krono is built for readers who also think. People who want to capture ideas as they come can do so as it’s not just designed to passively consume content. It suits commuters, students, writers, and knowledge workers who want a dedicated device for reading and note-taking that won’t pull them into social media rabbit holes.
The compact form factor makes it a natural fit for anyone who finds larger e-ink tablets impractical to carry daily, and the open Android platform appeals to readers who refuse to be locked into a single app or ecosystem. If you’ve been bouncing between a Kindle for reading and your phone for everything else, the Krono makes a strong case for consolidating those habits into one distraction-light device.
If the idea of a pocketable Android e-reader with a physical dial, AI-powered voice capture, and a sharp 300 PPI display sounds like your kind of tool, the DuRoBo Krono is worth a serious look at $279.99. Every unit also ships with a TPU case included at no extra cost, which makes the value proposition even easier to appreciate. Head over to DuRoBo’s product page to choose your color and shipping region, and see whether this is the focus device you’ve been waiting for.
results.summary:
The DuRoBo Krono is a new $279.99 pocket-sized Android 15 e-reader featuring a 6.13-inch E Ink display and a unique mechanical Smart Dial for distraction-free productivity and note-taking.

### Key Points
- The device runs on an octa-core processor with 6 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage, supporting full Google Play Store access.
- Its 6.13-inch E Ink Carta 1200 display offers a 300 PPI resolution and an adjustable dual-tone frontlight for various lighting conditions.
- The physical Smart Dial provides tactile control for page turning, brightness adjustment, and launching the Spark voice-to-text capture tool.
- Integrated AI features include the Libby AI assistant for quick lookups and automated summaries for recorded voice notes.
- The hardware includes an Axis lighting system with rear-facing "breathing lights" designed to help users maintain focus during reading sessions.

### Why it Matters
The Krono addresses the growing market demand for "distraction-light" technology by offering a dedicated, pocketable alternative to smartphones for readers and knowledge workers. By combining an open Android ecosystem with tactile hardware controls, it provides a versatile tool for users looking to consolidate their reading and note-taking habits.

results.title: Android May Soon Restrict On-Device ADB
results.author: Kitsumed
results.content:
Early Warning
Before we dive in, please note that this is not an official Google announcement. Instead, this is based on a recent, ongoing feature request on Google IssueTracker, in which a comment by one of the core ADB maintainers (Google employee) talked about restricting On-Device ADB connections to protect from “bad actors”.
Before you stop what you are doing to head over to that IssueTracker thread, please read this carefully:
If you plan to visit the issue tracker just to post low-quality comments (such as “Hey, don’t do this, I need Shizuku!”), complaints about monopoly, or insults, I highly recommend that you refrain from doing so. Spamming the thread will only cause Google developers to lock the issue, ignore valuable community feedback, or stop sharing public updates about this change entirely.
I think a change like this could benefit Google as it goes well along their new Sideloading changes, but I do not actively believe this is what is going on here. There is a true, valid reason behind this, and I think two different approach can be taken. We will talk about it in this blog post.
How You Can Help:
- If you have a unique use case: If you are directly affected and can write a detailed, constructive message explaining your workflow, providing links, or offering technical solutions/compromises, please, by all means, share your feedback in Google issue.
- If your use case has already been mentioned: You do not need to repeat it. Instead, simply click the +1 button in the top right corner of the Google IssueTracker to let Google know you are affected, and toggle notifications to stay updated on the discussion.
I am hesitant to make this blog post, as I fear it may overload the few developers that work on ADB. I am unsure if I should wait more and see what happens or hold it longer and see what approach they take. Waiting too long could also be bad… As of writing this, I am unsure when/if this post will release. I saw some recent updates on assignments which were given to the main guy who previously worked on ADB, so we will see what happens.
Introduction
Hi! I’m Kitsumed, developer of ShizuCallRecorder, a Shizuku based application. As you may have guessed by now, I would be affected by this change. Obviously, I would really like it if they do not proceed with it in a way that prevent loopback connections.
To talk briefly about myself, I made ShizuCallRecorder to help with some of my own disabilities. I can get by without it, but it’s much easier with it.
You could say I have a very unique use case, and I keep discovering other unusual ones, like this person on Reddit, who used my application to preserve the voicemail of a deceased loved one.
Call recording on Android is a complicated topic. There are countless user requests, an official attempt to add the feature in Android 11 that was later canceled, and many closed-source, privacy-invasive applications that use work-arounds.
I used to hear that many users with disabilities had to trade their privacy for an easier daily life. I guess that’s what people mean when they talk about those trade-offs.
Don’t even get me started on OEMs that force an audio warning such as “This call is being recorded,” when it’s in places where it’s not legally required. People often don’t react well to that, even if you explain why you’re recording the call, it gives a bad impression. To be honest, I probably wouldn’t react well to it either.
I’m sure most of you have a more “power-user” use of Shizuku or even use loopback ADB for developer tasks. I do those too, but I wanted to point out one of my unique use case.
Alright, back on the main topic. Before I explain what the proposed change is, I’m going to explain what is ADB for less technical users.
What’s ADB?
ADB, also called Android Debug Bridge, is protocol created by Google to let developers do developer things on Android devices…
Basically, it grant us a high level of privileges, give us access to a lot of sensible commands to tests how the phone and application behave. Useful stuff for any developers or power-users.
ADB was originally designed to work over a USB connection, but later expanded how it could works:
- USB: The original way. ADB communicates directly over a USB cable.
- TCP/IP: Introduced as a way to run ADB over a network using an IP address and port (typically port 5555). The connection carries ADB traffic in plain text and provides a YES/NO prompt as authentication. Can only be enabled once you already have an active ADB connection.
- Wireless Debugging (Wifi 1.0/2.0): Introduced in Android 11, it aims to improve the legacy TCP/IP workflow. It requires pairing the computer with the device using a pairing code or QR code, then establishes an authenticated and encrypted connection for subsequent ADB sessions. It does not require an active ADB connection to be enabled.
What’s a On-Device ADB connection?
ADB was originally intended to be used with two devices (simplified explanation): the Android device being debugged run the ADB Daemon (ADBD) and a separate developer machine run the ADB client. In practice, however, this setup is not always convenient. Some developers work directly from their Android device and do not have access to a second machine.
This led to usage of On-Device ADB (this is not a official term). By using a terminal emulator such as Termux, developers can run an ADB client directly on their phone and establish a connection to the local daemon (ADBD) server using either ADB TCP/IP or Wireless Debugging. Since both the client and server are running on the same device, the connection is made through the loopback address (127.0.0.1). That’s what I call On-Device ADB.
While this is a niche use case compared to how ADB intended to be used, it has led to the creation of projects such as libadb-android by MuntashirAkon and Shizuku by RikkaApps. These projects, along with many others, have created a large open-source community that made a wide range of tools for developers and power-users.
The proposed change
A new feature was made on Google IssuerTracker to allow developers to choose what interface ADBD (ADB server daemon) would listen to.
This feature was proposed following a major security issue identified as CVE-2026-0073, which allowed the Wireless ADB authentication process to be fully bypassed. What is proposed in this issue is actually a nice idea.
Right now, ADBD makes itself available on every network your phone is connected to. This feature request asks to let developers choose which interface is chosen, reducing the exposure.
The problem
The problem lies in the response from one of ADB core maintainers:
Connection to localhost has also been the source of exploit where app are using that socket to adbd to escalate their privileges.
What about we restrict to always only binding to wifi interface
wlan0?
Here, we can see that the employee talk about only allowing wlan0, the interface of the Wifi connection. Doing so would break many things, On-Device ADB, ADB via VPN, ADB via Ethernet, and many other unique developers setups.
Another issue I see here is the stance they seems to currently have on “On-Device ADB”. Their comment suggests that On-Device ADB is viewed primarily as an exploit bad actors can use to elevate privileges, yet there a lot of legitimate usages of on-device ADB. Developers themself uses it when they can’t access a computer.
While it can indeed be used to elevate privileges, a “malicious” application cannot do so alone. It requires multiples actions that MUST be perfomed by a human.
Why On-Device ADB Is Not Really Used by Bad Actors
A malicious application could use an on-device ADB connection to perform privilege escalation. However, it cannot establish one by itself.
To illustrate this, I’ve laid out the general limitations a bad actor would face in a few scenarios, similar to my comment on IssueTracker.
Scenario 1: General Android Users
- You install a malicious application.- ADB is disabled. ADBD is not running, and the application does not have the WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGSpermission, as it must be manually granted via ADB. No exploitation attempts are possible.
 
- ADB is disabled. ADBD is not running, and the application does not have the 
Scenario 2: A Developer on Android 11+ Using Wireless ADB
- You install a malicious application.
- You enable USB debugging, starting ADBD.
- You enable Wireless ADB. ADBD is now running on your phone and listening on all network interfaces.
- The application would need to perform the one-time pairing process. This requires the user to manually retrieve the one-time code from Settings and provide it. No exploitation attempts are possible.
Scenario 3: A Developer Using ADB over TCP/IP
- You install a malicious application.
- You enable USB debugging, starting ADBD.
- You connect via USB ADB to enable TCP/IP, then disconnect the USB cable.
- ADBD continues running and listens on all network interfaces.
- The application initiates a connection, causing an authorization prompt to appear on the screen. If the user selects No, the connection is rejected. No silent exploitation attempts are possible.
Conclusion
In a normal scenario, a bad actor cannot gain an ADB connection. It is only possible while the developer is actively using ADB on the device, because a bad actor cannot start ADBD by themselves.
However, if we return to a scenario such as CVE-2026-0073, exploitation would become possible in Scenarios 2 and 3, but only after the user has manually enabled USB debugging. As for scenario 3, it would also require the developer to MANUALLY enable TCP/IP. I can understand the motivation for preventing loopback connections by default, but not to fully prevents it.
There is a difference between preventing it by default and permanently preventing it. I think this should be something users can disable through a persistent setting. By this, I mean a toggle that survives a reboot (else it would make tools like Shizuku impracticals) and, ideally, cannot be read by third-party applications. Otherwise, developers would have to repeatedly disable it whenever banking apps or games detect that on-device ADB is availabl. That said, this part could be worked around once a application is manually granted WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS.
I think that justifying blocking it because a human could perform actions to allow it would be far-fetched. A human could also designate a malicious application as a device administrator or grant it Accessibility permissions, and yet we would not get rid of those features.
I believe it should be an assumed risk that disabling such a security feature enables on-device debugging while also exposing the device to the rare possibility of a future vulnerability. To me, the feature/risk ratio make sense here, as there is a real, legitimate usage.
Although it may have not been originally intended, On-Device ADB has enabled a niche ecosystem of developer and power-user tools, including projects such as App Manager, libadb-android, Canta, aShell, ShizuWall, ShizuCallRecorder and Shizuku.
To conclude, I would like to mention my conclusion in What Is Shizuku? How Does It Work? Security Implications?, where I said as a joke:
Here’s my closing thought: I can’t wait to see how they’ll justify disabling loopback ADB over TCP/IP connections on non-emulator devices and start requiring a Google account…
Well I guess they may indeed disable loopback ADB. Huh… I was almost 100% right on that one I guess. If you are a technical user, I invite you to give your feedback inside the issue here. Please don’t forget the early warning.
results.summary:
Google is considering restricting on-device Android Debug Bridge (ADB) connections to improve security, a move that could inadvertently disable popular power-user tools like Shizuku and various developer applications.

### Key Points
- Google developers are discussing limiting ADB daemon (ADBD) connections to the Wi-Fi interface (wlan0) to mitigate potential privilege escalation exploits.
- The proposed change would effectively block "on-device" ADB, where developers use terminal emulators to run ADB commands locally via the loopback address (127.0.0.1).
- Popular open-source projects, including Shizuku, aShell, and various call recording utilities, rely on this local loopback connection to function.
- Security concerns stem from CVE-2026-0073, which previously allowed attackers to bypass Wireless ADB authentication.
- Critics argue that malicious exploitation of on-device ADB requires significant manual user intervention, making a total ban unnecessary and overly restrictive for power users.

### Why it Matters
Restricting on-device ADB would disrupt a niche but vital ecosystem of tools that allow users to customize their devices and manage permissions without a secondary computer. This change highlights the ongoing tension between Google’s efforts to harden Android security and the needs of developers who rely on advanced system-level access.

results.title: Do tougher e-scooter laws work? What the evidence says
results.author: Sarah Burke
results.content:
Ireland is preparing to introduce wide-ranging new e-scooter laws, including compulsory helmets, registration and licensing, as ministers seek to tackle a growing number of serious injuries and strengthen enforcement.
It also plans to raise the minimum age from 16 to 18, the highest national age limit for e-scooter use in Europe.
While several European countries have already introduced similar measures, researchers still have limited evidence showing which regulations are most effective at reducing harm.
So, what does the evidence actually tell us?
How big is the e-scooter injury problem?
Ireland's proposed changes follow growing concern about serious injuries involving e-scooters, particularly among children.
Between June 2024 and May 2025, 12 children were admitted to Temple Street Hospital with traumatic brain injuries following e-scooter crashes. There was then a 50% increase on admissions since June 2025, with 18 children admitted between June 2025 and May 2026.
At least seven more have been admitted since then.
E-scooter crashes also accounted for more than one-third of all paediatric traumatic brain injury admissions to Temple Street's neurosurgery and rehabilitation services in 2026.
Among 30 children admitted with traumatic brain injuries linked to e-scooters between May 2024 and June 2026, every child suffered bleeding inside the skull, more than half required emergency neurosurgery and almost all had not been wearing a helmet.
In total, Children's Health Ireland recorded 1,130 emergency department attendances linked to e-scooters between January 2021 and August 2025, estimating that one to two children each day are currently presenting to its emergency departments with e-scooter-related injuries.
The Road Safety Authority has also recorded fatalities involving e-scooters. Three riders were killed on Irish roads in 2023, one died in 2024, and a further three e-scooter users died in 2025.
Ireland is not alone. According to the European Transport Safety Council (ETSC), 119 people were killed and 5,867 seriously injured in reported e-scooter collisions across Europe in 2022, the most recent year for which comparable data is available.
Those figures help explain why governments across Europe are under pressure to act. What remains less clear is which measures actually work.
What is Ireland planning to do?
The Government is proposing a phased package of new rules aimed at improving safety and strengthening enforcement.
Subject to Cabinet approval, compulsory helmets, high-visibility clothing and a ban on under 18s using e-scooters could come into effect as early as August.
Separate legislation expected from September would require privately owned e-scooters to be registered and riders to hold a licence.
Greater legal protections for Garda members involved in pursuing e-scooters and e-bikes, similar to those available to police officers in the UK, are also under consideration.
Ministers have also said an outright ban on e-scooters remains "on the table" if the new measures do not improve safety.
However, while many of the proposals have been announced, some of the practical details have yet to be decided.
For example, the Government has not yet explained how the registration system will operate, what type of licence riders would need or whether insurance requirements will also be introduced.
What evidence is there that tougher rules work?
Several European countries have already introduced measures similar to those now being considered in Ireland, including helmet requirements, registration systems, technical standards and minimum age limits.
However, researchers say the evidence supporting those measures is uneven.
Dudley Curtis, a spokesperson for the ETSC, said there is stronger evidence for some interventions than others.
"I think helmets is the one we've got the evidence for," Mr Curtis said.
"On the licensing and registration piece, I don’t think we know," he added.
"That doesn’t mean it’s not doing something positive, but we just don’t have the data on that yet."
Part of the challenge is that e-scooters are still a relatively new form of transport. Countries also record collisions and injuries differently, making direct comparisons difficult.
Mr Curtis said researchers do not have reliable data on how far e-scooters are being ridden or how many people are using them, making it difficult to accurately assess risk.
As a result, many governments are taking what researchers describe as a precautionary approach, introducing measures designed to reduce risk even where clear evidence of their effectiveness is still emerging.
Germany, for example, requires e-scooters to display an insurance sticker, while Spain has introduced technical certification requirements for newly sold scooters. Other countries have imposed helmet rules, speed limits and restrictions on where scooters can be used.
Germany illustrates how difficult it can be to judge whether regulations are working. Although it introduced one of Europe's earliest regulatory systems when e-scooters were legalised in 2019, collision numbers have continued to rise.
That does not necessarily mean the regulations have failed. More people are using e-scooters than when they were first legalised, meaning rising collision numbers alone cannot show whether riding has become more or less safe.

While app-based rental scooters are widely available in cities across countries such as Germany and Portugal, Irish riders predominantly use privately owned scooters, with shared rental schemes remaining limited.
"With those kinds of schemes, there is a possibility to have more control over the speed and some of these extra risk factors," Mr Curtis said.
By contrast, some privately owned e-scooters can reach speeds of 50 to 60 km/h, similar to a moped.
The ETSC is calling for mandatory technical standards across the EU, including a 20 km/h speed limiter, minimum braking requirements, stability standards and limits on acceleration.
Can regulation change behaviour?
Denmark introduced compulsory helmets for e-scooter riders in 2022, backed by fines of around €200, visible enforcement and a public awareness campaign.
In the Danish Road Safety Council's annual nationwide observational survey, around 21% of riders were observed wearing helmets prior to 2022.
Following the law’s introduction, that had increased to 69%, remaining at around two-thirds in subsequent years.
Mr Curtis said the effectiveness of a helmet requirement would depend heavily on whether riders believed it would be enforced.
"Are people going to feel like they’re going to be stopped and fined for not wearing a helmet?" he said.
"Because if people don’t feel that that’s likely to happen, then they may well not wear a helmet."
The Danish Road Safety Council concluded that helmet laws, backed by enforcement and financial penalties, can significantly increase helmet use.
However, they also cautioned that further research is needed to establish whether higher helmet use has translated into fewer injuries.
Will registration and licensing be enforceable?
A major reason the Government wants to introduce registration, and licensing is because privately owned e-scooters can be difficult to police.
Unlike cars or motorcycles, e-scooters are not currently registered. That means Gardaí often have no straightforward way of identifying who owns a scooter or tracing it back to an individual after an incident.
Minister of State at the Department of Transport Seán Canney has said one aim of the proposals is to establish who owns e-scooters, who is using them and who is responsible for selling them.
Enforcement would remain the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. According to the Department of Justice, Gardaí have already initiated 793 prosecutions involving e-scooters and seized 1,412 scooters so far in 2026.
Gardaí currently have four mobile dynamometers, which can test whether an e-scooter is capable of exceeding the legal maximum speed. Scooters found to exceed that limit can be seized and riders prosecuted.
Supporters of registration argue that it could make it easier for Gardaí to identify riders involved in collisions, dangerous driving incidents or other offences. However, several important questions remain unanswered.
The Government has not yet published exactly how the registration system would operate, how compliance would be monitored, or what penalties would apply if riders fail to register their scooters or obtain a licence. However, Cabinet is expected to discuss further details next week.
There is also a separate question about enforcement on the ground.
Registration may help Gardaí identify the owner of a scooter after an incident, but it does not necessarily solve the problem of stopping riders who refuse to comply with the rules.
The Department of Justice has said pursuing riders can create significant risks for Garda members, riders and the wider public. Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly has said he is examining specialist pursuit training for Garda members, while the Government is also considering whether additional legal protections may be needed when Gardaí carry out pursuits.
For riders wondering whether scooters could be confiscated, Gardaí already have powers to seize e-scooters in certain circumstances. However, the Government has not yet outlined how confiscation would fit into the proposed registration and licensing system.
What do transport safety experts recommend?
While much of the public debate in Ireland has focused on helmets, enforcement and registration, international transport experts say improving e-scooter safety is unlikely to depend on any single measure.
Instead, they argue that the greatest safety improvements come from combining regulation with safer road design, lower traffic speeds and vehicles that meet appropriate technical standards.
The ETSC recommends a combination of lower speed limits, minimum age requirements, helmet use, drink-riding restrictions and stronger technical standards for braking, lighting and vehicle stability.
The OECD's International Transport Forum reached a similar conclusion. Its review found that between 30% and 40% of e-scooter crashes involve poor road surfaces, suggesting infrastructure may be just as important as rider behaviour in determining safety outcomes.
Taken together, the evidence suggests Ireland's proposed measures could reduce some of the risks associated with e-scooters.
What it does not show is that any single intervention is likely to dramatically reduce injuries on its own.
Researchers increasingly view e-scooter safety as something that depends on a combination of regulation, enforcement, infrastructure, vehicle standards and rider behaviour.
Mr Curtis warned against focusing solely on riders and their vehicles while overlooking the roads on which they are travelling.
"We don’t have the right infrastructure for these types of vehicles. We don’t have the separated cycle paths everywhere we need them," he said.
"If you solve some of that infrastructure that works for bikes, you’re also solving it for e-scooters."
"Let’s not just put all the blame on these vehicles and the people riding them."
results.summary:
Ireland is introducing strict new e-scooter regulations, including mandatory helmets, licensing, and an age limit of 18, to address a significant rise in serious injuries and road fatalities.

### Key Points
- New laws will mandate helmets, high-visibility clothing, and a minimum age of 18 for all e-scooter riders.
- Legislation expected in September will require private e-scooter owners to register their vehicles and hold a valid licence.
- Between January 2021 and August 2025, Children's Health Ireland recorded 1,130 emergency department visits related to e-scooter incidents.
- Data from Temple Street Hospital shows that 30 children suffered traumatic brain injuries from e-scooter crashes between May 2024 and June 2026.
- An Garda Síochána has already initiated 793 prosecutions and seized 1,412 e-scooters during 2026.
- Experts suggest that while regulations are necessary, long-term safety also requires improved road infrastructure and standardized vehicle technical requirements.

### Why it Matters
These measures represent a precautionary shift in transport policy as the government attempts to curb a growing public health crisis involving traumatic brain injuries. The success of these rules will depend on consistent enforcement and whether they can effectively mitigate risks without discouraging the use of alternative, sustainable transport.
